stories.title: A Cancer Survivor's Big Win at Work
stories.headline_kid: A woman who beat cancer went to court after her boss wouldn't let her work in a way that helped her recover — and she won.
summary: A worker in Singapore had cancer and fought hard to recover. When she went back to work, she asked to work from home sometimes so she could rest and go for check-ups, since her body was still healing.
Her company did not agree to this. Things became so difficult at work that she felt she had no choice but to resign, even though she didn't really want to leave her job.
She decided to take her case to court, saying she was wrongfully forced out. This week, the court ruled in her favour, agreeing that she had been treated unfairly.

Lawyers say this case sends an important message: companies in Singapore need to think carefully about how they treat workers who are sick or recovering from illness, and try to support them instead of pushing them away.

lenses.me: It shows that if someone is unwell, they still deserve to be treated fairly and kindly, whether at school or at work.
lenses.family: If your parents or relatives ever get seriously ill, this case shows their workplace should try to support their recovery, not make things harder.
lenses.friends: Your friends' parents might work at companies that now think twice about how they treat staff who are sick.
lenses.nation: This court decision could change how Singapore companies handle workers recovering from serious illness in future.
lenses.world: It's part of a bigger conversation happening in many countries about fairness for workers dealing with health problems.

stories.title: How Will AI Change Grown-Ups' Jobs in Singapore?
stories.headline_kid: Singapore is planning how AI, or artificial intelligence, will change the way people work — so no one gets left behind.
summary: Singapore's government is working on something called the Economic Strategy Review. It's a big plan to figure out how the country's economy should grow in the future, especially with AI becoming more common at work.
AI is like a super-smart computer helper that can write, plan, and even make decisions. It's already being used in many offices to help people work faster.

But an expert warns that just having a national plan is not enough. Each job needs to be redesigned so workers actually know how to use AI well — a bit like giving someone a calculator but never teaching them how to press the buttons.

This matters because many parents' jobs could change as companies start using more AI. Singapore wants to make sure workers are trained properly, so AI helps them instead of confusing or replacing them.

lenses.me: The jobs you might do when you grow up could look very different because of AI — good preparation now really matters!
lenses.family: Your parents' workplaces might slowly start using more AI tools, and companies need to train them properly.
lenses.friends: Classmates might grow up to work alongside AI helpers in almost any career they choose.
lenses.nation: Singapore wants to lead in using AI wisely, so the whole country's economy stays strong and fair.
lenses.world: Many countries are racing to figure out how AI should be used at work — Singapore's approach could be an example for others.

compo_words.example: The company had to redesign how workers used the new AI tool.

compo_words.meaning: a change from one situation to another
compo_words.example: Singapore is preparing workers for the transition to using more AI.

stories.title: Why America's Money Troubles Could Affect Your Family Too
stories.headline_kid: The US government owes so much money that borrowing costs are spiking around the world — and that could even nudge up loan costs here.
summary: When governments need extra money, they borrow it by selling something called 'bonds' — a bit like an IOU note that promises to pay the money back later, plus a little extra called interest.

This week, the interest rates on US government bonds shot up to their highest levels in nearly 20 years, which worried investors a lot. To calm things down, the US Treasury (like America's money department) promised to sell even more of these long-term bonds.
That promise cheered up stock markets in Asia, including here, for a short while. But soon after, the worry returned, and stock markets fell again as bond troubles continued.

Why should you care? When a huge country like the US struggles with its borrowing, interest rates can rise everywhere — including for loans and mortgages in Singapore — which could make some things pricier for families.

lenses.me: It shows how money problems in one big country can quietly affect prices and loans even in your own home.
lenses.family: If interest rates rise, things like home loans could become a bit more expensive for families.
lenses.friends: Your friends' families might also feel small effects, like slightly pricier loans for cars or homes.
lenses.nation: Singapore's economy is connected to the world's biggest markets, so global money troubles can ripple here too.
lenses.world: This shows how connected all countries' economies are — one nation's borrowing troubles can affect the whole world.

compo_words.meaning: to put money into something hoping it grows
compo_words.example: Many people invest their savings to earn more money over time.

compo_words.meaning: to take money that must be paid back later
compo_words.example: Governments sometimes borrow money to build roads and schools.

compo_phrases.example: Interest rates shot up this week, worrying investors.

questions: Have you ever borrowed something and had to pay it back? How did that feel?
Why do you think it's important for countries to manage their borrowing carefully?

stories.title: China's Biggest Property Company Boss Gets Punished
stories.headline_kid: The man behind China's giant property company Evergrande, once its biggest homebuilder, has been fined and jailed after years of trouble.
summary: Evergrande used to be one of the biggest companies in China, building huge numbers of apartment blocks all across the country. To grow so fast, it borrowed enormous amounts of money.

In 2020, China's government made new rules to stop companies from borrowing too much in the property business. Evergrande suddenly struggled to pay back what it owed, and its troubles snowballed into a massive crisis.
This week, a court finally ruled on the long-running saga, ordering fines and jail time for Evergrande's founder, Hui Ka-yan.

This matters because it shows what can happen when a company borrows far more than it can handle. China's economy has been hurt by Evergrande's collapse, and since China trades closely with Singapore and many other countries, its economic troubles can be felt far beyond its borders.

lenses.me: It's a good reminder that borrowing more than you can pay back — even for grown-up companies — leads to serious trouble.
lenses.family: If your family has any savings or investments linked to China, this news could be relevant to keep an eye on.
lenses.friends: Your friends might have heard adults talking about property or stock market worries linked to China.
lenses.nation: Singapore trades a lot with China, so a slower Chinese economy can affect Singapore businesses too.
lenses.world: China is one of the world's largest economies, so its property troubles matter for the whole global economy.

compo_words.meaning: to suddenly fail or fall apart
compo_words.example: The company's finances began to collapse after years of heavy borrowing.

stories.title: Are Robots About to Get Super Smart Like Chatbots?
stories.headline_kid: A robot company boss in China says human-shaped robots are about to get a lot smarter — able to figure out almost any task you ask them to do.
summary: Unitree, a Chinese company that makes human-shaped robots, recently had a huge stock market debut. Its robots can already walk, dance, and do backflips!

The company's CEO says robots are getting close to a 'ChatGPT moment.' Remember how ChatGPT suddenly got amazingly good at chatting and answering questions? He believes robot 'brains' are about to make a similar giant leap.
If this happens, you might be able to simply tell a robot, using your voice, 'clean my room' or 'carry these bags,' and it would figure out how to do it — even in a place it has never been before.

Singapore already uses robots to clean floors at Changi Airport, deliver food in some neighbourhoods, and assist in hospitals. If robots really do become this smart, Singapore could use them for even more helpful jobs in the future.

lenses.me: You might grow up seeing robots doing everyday tasks around your home, school, or neighbourhood!
lenses.family: Robots could one day help your family with chores like cleaning or carrying heavy groceries.
lenses.friends: You and your friends might get to see or even try out smart robots at malls or science exhibitions.
lenses.nation: Singapore is already testing robots for cleaning and delivery, and could adopt smarter robots as this technology improves.
lenses.world: Countries everywhere are racing to build smarter robots, which could change how work gets done globally.

compo_words.example: Scientists hope for a breakthrough in robot technology soon.

compo_words.meaning: directions telling someone (or something) what to do
